parts.label: (a)
parts.text: With reference to the photoelectric effect, state what is meant by *work function energy*.

markscheme_points.text: energy (of photon) required to remove electron from a surface
or reference to minimum energy or reference to zero kinetic energy

hints: Hint 1: Think of one photon meeting one electron. Part of the photon energy is spent just getting the electron out of the metal, the rest can become kinetic energy.
Hint 2: Focus on the word minimum. What is the smallest photon energy that can still just release an electron with no speed left over?
parts.proper_answer: The minimum energy required to remove an electron from the metal surface, so that it is emitted with zero kinetic energy.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture what holds the electron in**
Electrons in a metal are attracted to the positive ions. To leave the surface and enter the vacuum they need to be given energy to break free. This is like needing a minimum push to climb out of a well.

Step 2: **Define the minimum escape energy**
The work function energy $\Phi$ is that minimum amount. If the incident photon supplies exactly $\Phi$, the electron just escapes with no kinetic energy left. Any extra photon energy above $\Phi$ appears as kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectron: $$hf = \Phi + E_{k,max}$$

parts.label: (b)(i)1.
parts.part_stem:
The work function energy of a clean metal surface is $5.5 \times 10^{-19} \text{J}$.

Electromagnetic radiation of wavelength $280 \text{nm}$ is incident on the metal surface. The metal is in a vacuum.

Calculate:

parts.label: (b)(i)2.
parts.text: 2. the maximum speed $v_{\text{MAX}}$ of the electrons emitted from the surface.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Explain why most of the emitted electrons will have a speed lower than $v_{\text{MAX}}$.

markscheme_points.text: energy is required to bring electron to the surface

hints: Hint 1: $v_{MAX}$ assumes the electron starts right at the surface. What if the electron starts deeper inside and has to travel out through other atoms?
parts.proper_answer: Most electrons originate below the surface and lose energy in collisions bringing them to the surface, so less energy remains as kinetic energy after escape.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Not all electrons start at the surface**
Only electrons emitted directly from the surface get the full $hf - \Phi$ as kinetic energy. Electrons deeper in the metal must first travel to the surface. On the way they collide with ions and other electrons and lose some energy as heat. So after paying the work function they have less than the maximum kinetic energy left, and hence a lower speed.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
The electromagnetic radiation incident on the metal surface may change in intensity or in frequency.

Complete Fig. 11.1 by inserting either '*increases*' or '*decreases*' or '*no change*' to describe the effects of the changes shown on the maximum speed and on the rate of emission of electrons.

{{figure:figure_11_1}}

Fig. 11.1
hints: Hint 1: Maximum speed comes from the energy of one photon, $hf$. Does changing the number of photons per second change the energy of each one?
Hint 2: Rate of emission counts how many electrons per second escape. At constant frequency, what does lower intensity mean for the number of photons arriving per second?
Hint 3: If frequency is increased, each photon carries more energy, so think what happens to $E_{k,max}$ and $v_{MAX}$ from $hf = \Phi + E_{k,max}$.
Hint 4: At constant intensity, total power is fixed. If each photon now carries more energy, what must happen to the number of photons per second and hence to the rate of electrons?
parts.proper_answer: Reduced intensity at constant frequency: maximum speed no change, rate of emission decreases. Increased frequency at constant intensity: maximum speed increases, rate of emission decreases.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Reduced intensity, constant frequency**
Frequency sets photon energy $hf$, so $E_{k,max}$ and $v_{MAX}$ are unchanged. Intensity is power per unit area, proportional to number of photons per second. Fewer photons means fewer one-to-one emissions, so the rate of emission decreases.

Step 2: **Increased frequency, constant intensity**
Larger $f$ gives larger $hf$. From $$E_{k,max} = hf - \Phi$$ the maximum kinetic energy is larger, so maximum speed increases. But intensity $I \approx N hf$ is fixed, where $N$ is photons per second. If $hf$ goes up, $N$ must go down to keep $I$ constant. Fewer photons per second means fewer emitted electrons per second, so the rate of emission decreases.

parts.label: (b)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Start with the light. You are given wavelength, but photon energy depends on frequency. How are wavelength, frequency and speed of light linked?
Hint 2: Convert the wavelength to SI units first. $280\text{ nm}$ means $280 \times 10^{-9}\text{ m}$. Keep $h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J s}$ and $c = 3.00 \times 10^{8}\text{ m s}^{-1}$ ready.
Hint 3: Compare your photon energy with the work function $5.5 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J}$. The difference is what is left for the electron after it escapes.
Hint 4: That leftover energy is the maximum kinetic energy, $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$. Recall the electron mass $m = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\text{ kg}$.
Hint 5: Rearrange to $v_{MAX} = \sqrt{2E_k/m}$ before putting numbers in, then check your speed is of order $10^5$ to $10^6\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the energy carried by one photon**
Light comes in packets. The energy of one packet depends on its wavelength: $$E = hf = \frac{hc}{\lambda}$$ Here $h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J s}$, $c = 3.00 \times 10^{8}\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and $\lambda = 280\text{ nm} = 280 \times 10^{-9}\text{ m}$. So: $$E = \frac{(6.63 \times 10^{-34})(3.00 \times 10^{8})}{280 \times 10^{-9}} \approx 7.10 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J}$$

Step 2: **Use the photoelectric energy balance**
One photon gives all its energy to one electron. Part pays the work function $\Phi = 5.5 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J}$, the rest becomes kinetic energy: $$E_{k,max} = hf - \Phi$$ $$E_{k,max} = (7.10 - 5.5) \times 10^{-19} = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J}$$ This is the maximum because it assumes the electron was at the surface and lost no other energy.

Step 3: **Convert kinetic energy to speed**
For the fastest electrons: $$\frac{1}{2}mv_{MAX}^2 = E_{k,max}$$ with $m = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\text{ kg}$. Rearranging: $$v_{MAX} = \sqrt{\frac{2E_{k,max}}{m}} = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}}{9.11 \times 10^{-31}}}$$ $$v_{MAX} \approx 5.9 \times 10^{5}\text{ m s}^{-1}$$
